subject: closed bank door
title: What If Every Bank Closed for Six Months? Ireland's Did, and Pubs Took Over

scenes.text: What if every bank in your country shut for six months? In 1970, Ireland's did.
On May 1, 1970, an industrial dispute closed most of the Irish banking system. It stayed shut until mid-November.
No deposits, no withdrawals, nowhere to cash a cheque. So people kept writing cheques anyway, and passed them on like banknotes.
A cheque is only as good as the person who signed it. The people who knew that best stood behind the bar. Pubs and shops became the country's credit checkers.
Cheques were signed over again and again, never cashed, moving from hand to hand for months.
After the banks reopened, it took until early 1971 to untangle. But the economy hadn't collapsed. For half a year, money was simply trust, and it held.

description:
What if a country's banks all closed for half a year? In Ireland it happened: an industrial dispute shut most of the banking system from 1 May to 17 November 1970.
People went on writing cheques, which were endorsed and passed along as a kind of currency. Publicans and shopkeepers, who knew their customers, judged whose cheques could be trusted. Banking was not back to normal until early 1971, yet a later study found no sign that retail sales had suffered, though businesses did have to divert staff to cope.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Ireland's banks also closed in 1966 and 1976, but 1970 was the longest. Would it work where you live, and what should we run through next?
